analyses.title: Improved Online Conformal Prediction via Strongly Adaptive Online Learning
analyses.research_question: Can online conformal prediction be made strongly adaptive so that prediction sets maintain useful coverage and efficiency across localized time intervals under changing or arbitrarily shifting data distributions?
analyses.methodology: The authors formulate Strongly Adaptive Online Conformal Prediction (SAOCP), a meta-algorithm that maintains multiple finite-lifetime online-learning experts operating on different active intervals, and instantiate those experts with Scale-Free Online Gradient Descent (SF-OGD). They prove strongly adaptive regret and coverage guarantees, including a near-optimal regret rate simultaneously over all interval lengths. Empirical evaluation covers multi-horizon forecasting on M4 and NN5 time-series datasets and image classification under sudden and gradual corruption shifts on TinyImageNet/TinyImageNet-C and ImageNet/ImageNet-C, using coverage, prediction-set size or width, local coverage error, and strongly adaptive regret.

key_findings.finding: SAOCP achieves strongly adaptive regret of order approximately sqrt(k) up to logarithmic factors simultaneously for every interval length k, whereas the compared FACI guarantee can be tuned to a comparable rate for a particular interval length but not all lengths simultaneously.

SF-OGD has a distribution-free empirical coverage-error bound that converges to zero, while SAOCP receives a distribution-free bound for a randomized expert-selection variant and stronger interval-wise coverage guarantees under additional distributional regularity assumptions.

Across the three M4 forecasting datasets, SAOCP maintained global coverage near the 0.9 target and consistently obtained the best or second-best interval width, local coverage error, and strongly adaptive regret across the tested base predictors.
Under sudden and gradual image-distribution shifts, SAOCP and SF-OGD kept local coverage closest to the 0.9 target, with the advantage most pronounced around abrupt change points.

Directly predicting the conformal radius, as done by SF-OGD and SAOCP, was empirically more robust than quantile-style parameterizations in several cases where the underlying forecasting model had relatively high prediction error.

limitations: The principal distribution-free coverage theorem for SAOCP is stated for a randomized variant that samples an expert rather than for the deterministic weighted-radius form used as the main algorithm.
The strongest interval-wise coverage result requires additional regularity assumptions and depends on temporal variation in the true quantiles.
The theoretical formulation assumes nested prediction sets and a bounded maximum radius parameter.
Empirical evaluation is confined to time-series forecasting and image corruption benchmarks rather than free-form generative models.
The experiments use specific benchmark shift processes, so they do not exhaust the range of non-stationary or adversarial changes that could occur in deployment.
The paper addresses calibration through prediction-set coverage rather than evidence completeness, omission detection, or selective abstention for long-form text.
raw_claims: SAOCP manages multiple experts whose active intervals are localized in time.
At most logarithmically many experts are active at a given time when the lifetime multiplier is constant.
SAOCP attains a near-optimal strongly adaptive regret rate simultaneously over all interval lengths.
SF-OGD's empirical coverage error converges toward the target without distributional assumptions.
The forecasting evaluation uses 5,111 time series across M4 and NN5.
Forecasting metrics include global coverage, median interval width, worst-case local coverage error, and strongly adaptive regret.
SAOCP outperforms the main adaptive baselines on localized coverage and regret across the reported M4 experiments.
Image experiments include both abrupt and gradual changes in corruption severity.
SAOCP and SF-OGD react more effectively to image-distribution change points than the slower-adapting baselines.
The authors provide experimental code in a public repository.

analyses.title: Overview of the TAC 2008 Update Summarization Task
analyses.research_question: How effectively can automatic systems produce concise summaries containing new information from a later document set when the reader is assumed to know an earlier set, and how well do automatic summary metrics reflect human judgments of that capability?
analyses.methodology: TAC 2008 defined 48 topics from the AQUAINT-2 English newswire collection; for each topic, 20 chronologically ordered documents were divided into an initial set of 10 and a later set of 10. Systems produced a 100-word initial summary and a 100-word update summary intended to avoid information already available from the earlier documents. All 71 submitted runs were scored with ROUGE and Basic Elements metrics, while 57 runs received manual evaluation for readability, overall responsiveness, and Pyramid content coverage; ANOVA, multiple-comparison tests, and correlation analyses were used to compare systems, humans, summary types, and metrics.

key_findings.finding: Human summaries were significantly better than automatic summaries on manual measures of readability, Pyramid content coverage, and overall responsiveness.
Human summarizers performed similarly on initial and update summaries, whereas automatic systems had greater difficulty selecting responsive content for the later update summaries.

The Pyramid evaluation explicitly rewarded coverage of weighted information units while giving no extra credit for repeating the same Summary Content Unit, thereby operationalizing both content completeness and non-redundancy.

ROUGE-2, ROUGE-SU4, and BE-HM correlated highly with manual evaluation for automatic summaries, and differences among their Pearson or Spearman correlations were not statistically significant at the 95 percent level.

Automatic overlap metrics failed to reproduce some important distinctions visible to manual evaluation, including the clear human-versus-system gap, and BE-HM failed to detect the aggregate degradation from initial to update summaries.

limitations: Only 57 of 71 submitted runs received the full manual evaluation.
Each topic's summaries were evaluated by a single assessor, who was also one of the human summarizers and usually the topic developer.
There were only eight human peers compared with many more automatic peers, making some human-side correlation estimates sparse.
The benchmark is restricted to English newswire, two fixed temporal batches, and 100-word summaries.
The two-cycle setup does not represent indefinitely evolving streams, superseded facts, or long-running work-item state.
ROUGE and Basic Elements depend heavily on lexical or structural overlap and can penalize valid paraphrases.
The task models a generic reader rather than adaptive user-specific priorities or personalized reminder value.
raw_claims: Each topic contained two chronological sets of ten newswire documents.
The second 100-word summary was supposed to communicate information that was new relative to the first document set.
Forty-eight evaluation topics were constructed by eight NIST assessors.
Seventy-one submitted runs received automatic ROUGE and Basic Elements scores.
Fifty-seven submitted runs received manual readability, content, and responsiveness evaluation.
Pyramid content units were weighted by how many reference summaries expressed the same information.
Repeated expression of the same Pyramid content unit did not earn additional credit.
Human summaries clearly outperformed automatic summaries on the manual quality measures.
Automatic systems performed worse on update summaries than on initial summaries, while the same degradation was not observed for human summaries.
ROUGE and Basic Elements correlations alone did not capture all of the discriminative behavior of human evaluation.

analyses.title: Evaluating LLM Uncertainty in Long-Form Generation Using Deterministic Ground Truth
analyses.research_question: How can uncertainty in long-form LLM generation be evaluated at fine-grained resolution without noisy external judges, and what does such evaluation reveal about correctness propagation, calibration, confidence ranking, and reasoning?
analyses.methodology: The paper introduces SALT, a procedurally generated benchmark in which long outputs have deterministic reference answers that can be decomposed into task-aligned atomic and line units. Six tasks with complete model coverage provide 54,797 evaluated atoms across mathematics, logic, code, DNA translation, and multi-needle retrieval, with additional ARC-AGI and maze experiments reported separately; more than 50 LLMs are evaluated. Unit correctness is determined against deterministic ground truth, while uncertainty is measured using precision, expected calibration error, Macro- and Micro-AUROC, PRR, multiple logit- and verbalization-based confidence functions, post-hoc calibration schemes, paired statistical tests, and controlled prefix interventions.

key_findings.finding: Fine-grained confidence ranking deteriorates sharply at atomic resolution: many models' atomic Micro-AUROC values lie only modestly above chance, while line-level units exhibit substantially clearer ranking signal.

Long-form correctness is path-dependent: errors in the generated prefix strongly reduce future correctness, while answer-context length contributes a separate but bounded degradation that saturates relatively early.

Reasoning interventions improved answer precision but reduced the model's ability to rank its own correct and incorrect units by confidence; the reported paired analysis found a 23.3 percent relative AUROC degradation alongside accuracy gains.

Logit-derived confidence functions significantly outperformed verbalized confidence across both calibration and ranking comparisons, but the best confidence function depended on which uncertainty property was being measured.
Post-hoc binned calibration minimized ECE but harmed ranking, demonstrating that calibration quality and error-ranking quality can move in opposite directions.

Uncertainty-estimation rankings transferred only conditionally to conventional benchmarks: line-level agreement was stronger for AIME, while agreement with MMLU-Pro was weak and depended on the calibration regime.

limitations: SALT's deterministic tasks are deliberately structured and synthetic, so they do not reproduce the ambiguity, conflicting evidence, source attribution, and open-ended semantics of real-world free-form reports.
Strict deterministic unit matching is much easier to define than factual correctness for naturally written multi-source claims.
The benchmark studies uncertainty on generated answer units but does not directly evaluate evidence completeness or whether decision-relevant source facts were omitted.
It does not directly model temporal evidence evolution, version supersession, or non-stationary source distributions.
ARC-AGI and Maze had incomplete model coverage because of compute constraints and were excluded from aggregate main-body results.
Transfer to external benchmarks was conditional, with weak agreement in some benchmark and granularity combinations.
The work evaluates uncertainty metrics rather than providing formal selective-prediction or risk-control guarantees under distribution shift.
raw_claims: SALT uses deterministic long-form targets so correctness labels do not depend on human or LLM judges.
The six tasks used for the aggregate evaluation contain 54,797 atomic units.
The study evaluates more than 50 language models.
Correctness tends to decrease as a generated response progresses.
The correctness of earlier generated units is strongly associated with the correctness of later units.
Controlled interventions separate error propagation from the effect of answer-context length.
Atomic-level confidence ranking is substantially weaker than line-level ranking.
Reasoning improves answer accuracy while degrading confidence-based discrimination between correct and incorrect units.
Logit-based uncertainty signals outperform verbalized confidence signals in the reported comparisons.
Optimizing post-hoc calibration for low ECE can reduce AUROC ranking quality.
The released repository includes reproduction datasets and procedural dataset generators.

analyses.title: Overview of the TREC 2016 Real-Time Summarization Track
analyses.research_question: How should systems that continuously monitor a live social-media stream for prospective information needs be evaluated for relevance, novelty, redundancy, and timeliness in both immediate push-notification and periodic digest settings?
analyses.methodology: TREC 2016 evaluated systems operating on Twitter's live sample stream during a ten-day period using prospective interest profiles. Scenario A systems could send up to ten push notifications per profile per day and were evaluated through an online broker that immediately delivered submitted tweets to mobile assessors, who labeled them relevant, redundant, or not relevant; Scenario B systems produced larger daily batches resembling email digests. NIST also performed pooled offline assessment and clustering of tweets into information facets, and the track deliberately separated output-quality metrics such as Expected Gain, normalized Cumulative Gain, Gain Minus Pain, precision, and nDCG from latency measurements. Scenario A received 41 runs from 18 groups and Scenario B received 40 runs from 15 groups.

key_findings.finding: The track demonstrated a workable real-time evaluation architecture in which live system outputs could be routed immediately to mobile assessors and judged in the temporal context in which notifications were received.
Treating redundant tweets separately from relevant novel tweets allowed the evaluation to explicitly penalize repeated information and measure the value of newly surfaced content.
key_findings.section: 2.4 Online Judgments and 2.5.1 Scenario A Metrics

key_findings.finding: Across submitted runs, the authors observed no strong relationship between output-quality metrics and notification latency, contrary to the intuitive expectation that waiting longer to accumulate evidence would necessarily improve quality.
Daily digest systems did not, as a group, outperform push-notification systems on quality metrics despite having the opportunity to accumulate evidence over an entire day.

Metrics that reward correctly remaining silent made an empty or low-output strategy surprisingly competitive in some settings, showing the importance of evaluating whether a system knows when no valuable new update exists.
key_findings.section: 2.5.1 Scenario A Metrics and 3.1 Scenario A

key_findings.finding: A strong 2015 baseline fell around the middle of the 2016 result set, which the authors interpreted as evidence of progress by participating systems.

limitations: Only 13 of the 18 recruited online assessors ultimately supplied judgments, and assessor response rates were highly uneven.
Many pushed tweets remained unjudged, so online judgments were sparse relative to the total notification volume.
The mobile evaluation application had deployment and display problems that affected some assessors.
A clock-skew problem caused some broker timestamps to precede tweet publication times, and the authors applied a uniform 139-second correction after the infrastructure had already been shut down.
The evaluation did not model notification restrictions such as avoiding nighttime interruptions.
Defining digest days in UTC ignored users' local time zones and reading habits.
The first-year infrastructure did not support user-submitted interest profiles or online feedback to participating systems.
The study was limited to Twitter's sample stream, a short evaluation period, and prospective topics constructed in advance rather than longitudinal workplace work-item state.
The setup measured interest-profile relevance rather than adaptive personalization learned from an individual user's evolving priorities.
raw_claims: The track evaluated systems on prospective information needs over a live Twitter stream.
Push notifications were expected to be relevant, novel, and timely.
Daily digests emphasized relevance and novelty while tolerating much greater latency.
Online assessors labeled notifications as relevant, redundant, or not relevant.
A redundant notification contained relevant information that was substantively similar to information the assessor had already seen.
Forty-one Scenario A runs from eighteen groups produced more than 160,000 pushed tweets.
Thirteen assessors supplied 12,115 online judgments.
Quality and latency were evaluated separately rather than collapsed into a single score.
The experiment did not reveal a strong empirical quality-latency trade-off.
Daily digest runs did not show the expected quality advantage over real-time push runs.
The online evaluation infrastructure was released as open-source software.

analyses.title: On the Evaluation of Machine-Generated Reports
analyses.research_question: How can long-form machine-generated reports for complex information needs be evaluated jointly for completeness, factual support, citation correctness, responsiveness, and reuse across future systems?
analyses.methodology: This is a perspective and framework paper rather than a comparative system experiment. The authors synthesize ideas from information retrieval, summarization, question answering, and RAG evaluation into ARGUE, where a system receives a document collection and a detailed report request and must produce a cited report. Human assessors define question-answer information nuggets and bind acceptable nugget answers to supporting source elements; completeness is measured primarily as nugget recall, while accuracy and verifiability are measured through report-segment precision and citation support. The paper supplies an illustrative manually scored example and discusses pooling, interactive search, active learning, and eventual automation of assessment decisions.

key_findings.finding: ARGUE operationalizes report completeness as recall over assessor-defined information nuggets, with a nugget counted as covered only when the report states it with the required supporting citation evidence.

The framework separately evaluates segment-level precision, allowing unsupported citations, missing required citations, and unattested claims to be penalized while avoiding conflation with missing-content errors.
Repeated support for the same information nugget counts only once toward recall, giving the framework an explicit mechanism for separating coverage from repetition.

Report requests can encode user background, required content, known background information, length constraints, and temporal source windows, making the intended information need substantially richer than a conventional short retrieval query.

The framework explicitly permits a nugget representing a requested fact that is absent from the collection, allowing evaluation of whether the report correctly states that requested evidence is unavailable.
The claim that most assessment decisions can be automated reasonably well with current technology is proposed but is not validated by an empirical automation study in this paper.

The worked example demonstrates the accounting rules for precision and recall, but it does not establish empirical reliability, discriminative power, or system-ranking validity for ARGUE at benchmark scale.

limitations: The paper proposes a conceptual evaluation framework and illustrative example rather than reporting a large-scale validation study.
ARGUE restricts citations to a predefined document collection and cannot directly evaluate information whose evidence lies outside that collection.
The framework assumes source documents are truthful; validating source truthfulness is explicitly outside its scope.
Creating report requests, nuggets, acceptable answers, and document-to-nugget mappings requires substantial expert assessment effort.
Full collection annotation is impractical, so incomplete discovery of supporting documents or acceptable nugget answers can threaten reusability.
Determining what information is essential enough to become a nugget remains an assessor judgment and therefore embeds subjectivity.
Simple question-answer nuggets are less natural for information that must be expressed across multiple sentences or synthesized from multiple documents.
The framework is better suited to evidence-grounded informative reporting than to reports whose purpose is to produce novel analysis.

Although temporal-window constraints can be included in report requests, the framework does not itself model evolving evidence state, supersession, or longitudinal versions across repeated report cycles.
The paper does not address calibrated abstention or formal selective-risk guarantees under distribution shift.
raw_claims: ARGUE treats a report as a response to an explicitly specified information need supported by a bounded source collection.
A report request may include a user story, problem statement, background information, and constraints such as a source time window.
Human-created evaluation data is intended to reduce circularity between generative systems and their evaluators.
Required report content is represented through question-answer information nuggets.
Nugget answers are linked to source documents that attest the information.
Recall measures the proportion of required nuggets correctly represented with supporting citations.
Precision is computed over report segments and reflects whether their cited evidence supports their claims.
A repeated nugget contributes only once to recall.
Claims lacking required citations are penalized under the proposed scoring rules.
The framework can represent an explicitly requested but unattested fact as an absence nugget.
The illustrative example obtains full precision while missing two of five nuggets, showing why precision and completeness must be scored separately.
The authors regard responsiveness, grounding, verifiability, completeness, and reusability as core requirements for evaluating generated reports.
